title: #75 Always Frame and Reframe When Doing a Call and Respond
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton revisits his "Explain, Frame and Reframe" structure for Call and Respond, using a classroom observation to show why the "Reframe" step matters. A teacher taught the triangle-area formula by explaining it, then repeatedly framing a sentence stem for students to complete in unison. Barton tested understanding afterward: three students could all state the full formula when asked directly, but when he instead asked what "half multiplied by the base multiplied by the perpendicular height" gives you, only one could answer. He attributes the gap to students having only ever practiced completing the second half of the sentence, so that portion became isolated and disconnected from its meaning -- their knowledge was "fragmented" rather than integrated. The fix is to add a Reframe step that flips the sentence around, so students practice recalling the relationship in both directions rather than only the one direction rehearsed by the original Frame.
points: A Call and Respond routine that only ever frames a sentence stem in one direction risks producing "fragmented" knowledge -- students can complete the stem but can't recognise the same fact stated the other way round.
Barton's live test (asking students to state the formula vs. asking what the described calculation yields) turned an assumption of secure understanding into visible evidence of a gap.
The fix -- Reframe -- is a small structural addition (flip the sentence, drill the reverse direction) rather than a new technique, extending the existing Explain-Frame model rather than replacing it.

The tip implies a broader caution for any chant-and-respond routine: repeated recitation of one phrasing can create an illusion of understanding that doesn't transfer to an equivalent phrasing of the same fact.
quotes: I have written previously about why I like to do Explain, Frame and Reframe when doing Call and Respond. Recently, I saw a lesson that reminded me just how vital the Reframe part is.
I chose three students and asked them what the formula to work out the area of a triangle is. All three could tell me.
I then chose another three students and asked them what half multiplied by the base multiplied by the perpendicular height gives us. Only one could tell me.
Because students had only been asked to repeat the second half of the sentence, this was the only part that had been internalised. Their knowledge was fragmented.
Explain: The formula to work out the area of a triangle is half multiplied by the base multiplied by the perpendicular height.
He repeated this a few more times, and then moved onto a worked example that used this fact.
